text: Now something a little different. Refusing a letter on purpose, the two hundred limit. React puts back whatever state says. So can our code refuse a letter on purpose? Yes, it can. Our count already promises a limit of two hundred characters. So let's make the box keep that promise. We add one check to the message handler. On line seven of ContactForm.jsx, handleMessageChange takes e. Line eight is the new check. If e.target.value.length is less than or equal to two hundred. The note says it saves the text only while it fits. Inside that if, line nine calls set message with e.target.value. And lines ten and eleven just close the if and the function. Suppose the box already holds two hundred characters and the user types one more. Here's what happens. The browser puts the extra letter into the box. React calls handleMessageChange. The new text is two hundred and one characters long, so the handler does not call set message. Message still holds the two hundred characters, so React writes those two hundred characters back into the box, and the extra letter disappears. This is the freeze from the start of this principle used on purpose. The box accepts a letter only when our code saves it. And one more rule about the handler. It must save e.target.value right away. The handler has two more rules. It must save the text right away, and it must save exactly e.target.value. Here is a name handler that breaks the first rule. It saves the text later inside a timer. This is a name box whose handler saves the text later. Line one starts handleNameChange taking e. On line two, instead of saving, it calls setTimeout. Inside, an arrow function calls setName with e.target.value, and the wait is one hundred milliseconds. The note there warns, wrong. The state waits, but React puts the old text back right away. And on line five, the input has value equals name and onChange equals handleNameChange, both in curly braces. The user types, and the box still refuses every letter. The handler does run, so why? Here is the order. The user presses a key, and the browser shows the letter in the box. React calls handleNameChange, but the handler only starts a timer. The handler ends, and name still holds the old text. State did not change. So React writes the old text back into the box. A moment later, the timer runs and reads e.target.value. That is the same box, and it now holds the old text again. So setName saves the old text, and nothing changes. This box refuses letters just like a box with no onChange. This time, though, the console stays quiet because the box does have a handler. React's documentation says the state update cannot wait. It must happen inside the handler right away. The second rule is broken by a handler that saves a changed copy of the text. One example is a handler that turns every letter into a capital with to uppercase. The browser has just shown one text, and React then writes a different text into the box. React's documentation lists this as a cause of a caret that jumps around while the user types. So keep the handler simple. Save exactly e.target.value right away. And if you need to refuse a letter, refuse the whole change with an if, just as the two hundred limit does. Let's gather principle three into one place. Readonly value without onChange freezes the box. Every box with value also needs an onChange handler that saves the new text exactly as typed right away. With value, React writes the state into the box after every key. If no handler saves the new letter, state never changes. So React puts the old text back, and the console shows the readonly field error. The same freeze happens when the handler waits inside a timer, and a box that should be frozen on purpose says so with readonly. So do this. An input with value equals name and onChange calling setName with e.target.value. Each letter reaches state, so it stays. And don't do this. An input with value equals name and nothing else. No onChange. So React puts the old text back after every key.
